source_text: EVANGELICA praecepta, fratres dilectissimi, nihil aliud sunt quam magisteria divina, fundamenta aedificandae spei, firmamenta corroborandae fidei, nutrimenta fovendi cordis, gubernacula dirigendi itineris, praesidia obtinendae salutis; quae, dum dociles credentium mentes in terris instruunt, ad coelestia regna perducunt. Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione? Sit autem orantibus sermo et precatio cum disciplina, quietem continens et pudorem. Cogitemus nos sub conspectu Dei stare. Placendum est divinis oculis et habitu corporis et modo vocis. Nam, ut impudentis est clamoribus strepere, ita contra congruit verecundo modestis precibus orare. Denique magisterio suo Dominus secreto orare nos praecepit, in abditis et semotis locis, in cubiculis ipsis, quod magis convenit fidei; ut sciamus Deum ubique esse praesentem, audire omnes et videre, et majestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quoque et occulta penetrare, sicut scriptum est: Ego Deus approximans, et non Deus de longinquo. Si absconditus fuerit homo in absconditis, ego ergo non videbo eum? Nonne coelum et terram ego impleo? Et iterum: In omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos. Et quando in unum cum fratribus convenimus, et sacrificia divina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus, verecundiae et disciplinae memores esse debemus, non passim ventilare preces nostras inconditis vocibus, nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosa loquacitate jactare, quia Deus non vocis sed cordis auditor est. Nec admonendus est clamoribus qui cogitationes hominum videt, probante Domino et dicente: Quid cogitatis nequam in cordibus vestris? Et alio loco: Et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis.
pass_a_gloss: The evangelical precepts, most beloved brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings, foundations for building hope, reinforcements for strengthening faith, nourishments for fostering the heart, guides for directing our journey, and defenses for obtaining salvation; which, while instructing the minds of believers on earth, lead them to the heavenly kingdom. God wanted to be called and heard by His servants, the prophets, in many ways; but how much greater are the things that the Son speaks, which the Word of God, who was in the prophets, testifies with His own voice, no longer commanding that a way be prepared for Him to come, but coming Himself and opening and showing us the way, so that we, who were previously wandering in the darkness of death, ignorant and blind, might, enlightened by the light of grace, hold to the path of life with the Lord as our guide and director. Among other salutary admonitions and divine precepts by which He consults the salvation of His people, He also gave the form of prayer, teaching and instructing us what to pray for, He who gave us life, taught us to pray, with the same kindness by which He deigned to give and confer other things upon us, so that, while we speak to the Father with the prayer and supplication that the Son taught us, we may be heard more easily. He had already foretold that the hour would come when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, and He fulfilled what He had promised earlier, so that we, having perceived the spirit and truth from His sanctification, may truly and spiritually worship Him in tradition as well. For what prayer can be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What prayer can be more true before the Father than the one spoken by the Son, who is the Truth, from His own mouth? So that to pray otherwise than He taught is not only ignorance but also guilt, when He Himself said: You reject the commandment of God to establish your own tradition. Let us pray, therefore, most beloved brothers, as God, our teacher, taught us. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what is His, to ascend to His ears with the prayer of Christ. Let the Father recognize the words of His Son when we make our prayer. He who dwells within our breast should also be in our voice. And when we have Him as our advocate with the Father for our sins, when we sinners ask for forgiveness for our offenses, let us pronounce the words of our advocate. For when He says that whatever we ask of the Father in His name, He will give us, how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask for in the name of Christ if we ask with His own prayer? Let our speech and prayer, however, be with discipline, containing quiet and modesty. Let us consider that we stand before the eyes of God. We must please the divine eyes with both the posture of our body and the manner of our voice. For just as it is shameless to cry out with loud clamor, so it is fitting to pray with modest and reverent prayers. Finally, our Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and remote places, in our own chambers, which is more fitting for faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears all, and sees all, and with the fullness of His majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places, as it is written: I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar. If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? And again: The eyes of God watch over both the good and the evil in every place. And when we gather with our brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we should be mindful of modesty and discipline, not scattering our prayers everywhere with uncontrolled voices, nor boasting our petition to God with tumultuous loquacity, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Nor does He need to be reminded with clamor, who sees the thoughts of men, as the Lord proves and says: Why do you think evil in your hearts? And in another place: And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and the heart.

pass_b_english: The evangelical precepts, most beloved brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings: foundations for building hope, reinforcements for strengthening faith, nourishment for fostering the heart, guides for directing our journey, and defenses for obtaining salvation. While they instruct the minds of believers on earth, they lead them to the heavenly kingdom. God wanted to be called and heard through his servants the prophets in many ways; but how much greater are the things the Son speaks! The Word of God, who was in the prophets, now testifies with his own voice, no longer commanding that a way be prepared for his coming, but coming himself, opening the way, and showing it to us. He did this so that we — who were previously wandering in the darkness of death, ignorant and blind — might, enlightened by the light of grace, hold to the path of life with the Lord as our guide and director. (Jeremiah 23:23-24)

Among his other salutary admonitions and divine precepts by which he provides for his people's salvation, he also gave us the form of prayer, teaching and instructing us what to ask for. He who gave us life taught us to pray, with the same kindness by which he deigned to give and confer all other gifts, so that when we speak to the Father with the prayer and supplication the Son taught us, we may be heard more easily. He had already foretold that the hour would come when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, and he fulfilled what he had promised, so that we — having received the spirit and truth from his sanctification — may truly and spiritually worship him in tradition as well. (Jeremiah 23:24)

For what prayer can be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What prayer can be more true before the Father than the one spoken by the Son, who is the Truth, from his own mouth? Therefore, to pray otherwise than he taught is not only ignorance but also guilt, when he himself said: "You reject the commandment of God to establish your own tradition." Let us pray, then, most beloved brothers, as God our teacher taught us. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what is his own, to ascend to his ears with the prayer of Christ. Let the Father recognize the words of his Son when we make our prayer. He who dwells within our breast should also be in our voice. And when we have him as our advocate with the Father for our sins — we sinners asking for our offenses — let us pronounce the words of our advocate. For when he says that whatever we ask of the Father in his name he will give us, how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask for in the name of Christ if we ask with his own prayer? (Jeremiah 23:24)

Let our speech and prayer, however, be marked by discipline, keeping quiet and modesty. Let us consider that we stand before the eyes of God. We must please the divine eyes with both the posture of our body and the manner of our voice. For just as it is shameless to cry out with loud clamor, so it is fitting for the reverent to pray with modest prayers. Finally, our Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and remote places, in our own chambers, which is more fitting for faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears all, and sees all, and with the fullness of his majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places, as it is written: "I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar. If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" And again: "The eyes of God watch over both the good and the evil in every place." (Psalm 33:15)

And when we gather with our brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we should be mindful of modesty and discipline, not scattering our prayers everywhere with uncontrolled voices, nor pressing our petition upon God with tumultuous loquacity, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Nor does he need to be reminded by clamor, he who sees the thoughts of men, as the Lord proves and says: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" And in another place: "And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and the heart." (Revelation 2:23)
